newsitem.title: INDIA: India pledges not to ease corruption battle.
newsitem.headline: India pledges not to ease corruption battle.

text.p: The Indian government on Tuesday promised an unrelenting fight against corruption as Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral faced stiff criticism for abruptly transferring the federal police chief to a new job.
Critics accused Gujral of bowing to political pressure when he shifted Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) director Joginder Singh to the Home (Interior) Ministry on Monday.

They said the sudden decision to transfer Singh, who had led a high-profile campaign against political corruption and spearheaded a criminal probe into the chief of Gujral's party, sent the wrong signal at the wrong time.

"It was improper and open to misintepretation," Communist Party of India national secretary D. Raja told Reuters. "The prime minister should ensure that there is no interference in the CBI's work and the ongoing judicial process."

Gujral's Janata Dal party faces a potential split following the indictment of its president, Laloo Prasad Yadav, in a $280-million corruption case involving alleged siphoning-off of animal welfare funds. The CBI is prosecuting Yadav.
Yadav, who is chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, has said he is innocent and has steadfastly refused to step down as either state or party leader.

In Patna, the opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) filed a contempt of court petition in the local high court in protest against Singh's transfer, alleging an "unholy alliance" between Gujral and Yadav.
It said Singh's transfer violated a promise to the court last August that investigators should not be move without the court's permission.
"He (Singh) cannot be transferred or removed without the consent of the court," the BJP's general secretary for Bihar, Saryu Roy, told reporters.

The biggest group in Gujral's 15-party coalition, Janata Dal, is set to elect a leader on Thursday but Yadav's supporters decided to boycott the vote. They say a Yadav ally must be reinstated on a panel of poll observers and the voters' list must be adjusted.
The upheaval in Gujral's party has shaken the ruling alliance barely two months after he assumed power following a month-long political crisis.

A government spokesman dismissed claims that Gujral had transferred Singh, who took over the CBI only 11 months ago, to appease critics in Janata Dal and the Congress party who may want a slowdown in the corruption investigations.

"There will be no let-up in any investigation undertaken by the CBI irrespective of the status of the person, even regarding the cases in Bihar," the spokesman said. "The present pace will continue. There will be no change."
Officials said Gujral was upset that under Singh, the CBI's cases were played out in detail in the press but the agency had trouble winning convictions.

They cited an $18-million money-laundering case, alleged to involve more than 100 politicians and bureaucrats, which has begun to unravel for lack of evidence. Former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao was recently acquitted in a forgery case.
"We should not be conducting media trials, especially if the cases do not gel," the official said.
